**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering leadership
**From:** Infrastructure team
**Re:** Hardware expansion decision for the inference cluster

**Summary and recommendation**

We recommend that we spend the next quarter improving utilisation of the hardware we already own before committing to any new purchases. Our current fleet runs at roughly 30–35% average utilisation, with sharp peaks that make it *feel* perpetually saturated. The gap between how busy the cluster looks at 10 a.m. and how idle it is overnight is where our real capacity lives. Buying more hardware now would lock in capital against a demand curve we cannot yet predict, while the cheaper, reversible option — better scheduling, batching, and workload shaping — is only partially explored. If utilisation work stalls or demand genuinely outpaces us, we can still buy in Q3 with better information and, likely, better prices.

**The cost picture**

The purchase option is not enormous in absolute terms — two additional nodes would be a mid-five-figure commitment including networking and power — but it is the recurring costs that concern me. Colocation, maintenance contracts, and the engineering time to integrate and monitor new hardware are ongoing, and they compound. More importantly, the purchase is largely irreversible. GPUs depreciate quickly, our procurement cycle is slow, and reselling specialised hardware is a hassle we would rather avoid. Utilisation work, by contrast, costs engineering time we mostly already have, and every improvement is a permanent gain in efficiency that carries forward regardless of what we later decide about capacity. In option terms, improving utilisation preserves our ability to buy later; buying now forecloses the option of not needing to.

**Latency and the real bottleneck**

The strongest argument for buying is latency. Our p99 response times degrade badly during the morning peak, and a couple of teams have complained that batch jobs queued behind interactive traffic make their experiments feel sluggish. That pain is real. But when we traced it, much of the latency came from scheduling policy, not raw capacity: interactive requests waiting behind long batch jobs, models loaded and evicted repeatedly because we lack a coherent memory budget, and batch sizes tuned conservatively months ago. Fixing these is exactly the kind of work that raises effective capacity *and* cuts tail latency simultaneously. If we buy hardware without fixing scheduling, we will simply reproduce the same pathology on a larger fleet at higher cost.

**Reliability**

Reliability cuts both ways. Right now, a single node failure removes a meaningful fraction of our capacity, which is a genuine argument for more machines. But adding nodes without better failover and load-shedding logic just spreads the same fragility across more hardware. The utilisation work includes building proper queueing and graceful degradation, which improves reliability directly. A fleet that can shed load intelligently and rebalance work is more robust than a bigger fleet that cannot. We should also be honest that our monitoring of per-node health is thin; that is a cheap fix that belongs in this quarter regardless.

**Opportunity cost**

The scarcest resource here is not money but engineer attention. The same two or three people who would integrate new hardware are the ones best placed to do the scheduling and batching work. If we buy machines, we will spend a quarter on procurement, installation, and migration, and the underlying inefficiencies will still be there, now amortised across more silicon. If we spend that quarter on utilisation, we either solve the problem or we learn precisely what our true ceiling is — which makes any subsequent purchase better targeted. There is also an opportunity cost to the business: capital tied up in idle GPUs is capital not available for the data licensing work several of us think is the actual bottleneck on model quality.

**Uncertainty**

I want to be clear about what we do not know. Demand may grow faster than we forecast, particularly if the customer-facing pilot ships in the autumn. Some utilisation gains may prove illusory — peak-hour demand may be irreducible, and there is a floor below which idle capacity cannot be squeezed. And utilisation work has a soft deadline problem: it is easy to defer indefinitely, whereas a purchase order forces the issue. To guard against this, we should set explicit success criteria now: if by the end of the quarter p99 latency at peak has not improved materially, or utilisation has not risen above 55%, we escalate the purchase request with our findings attached.

**Conclusion**

Buy later, but only if the numbers then justify it. Spend this quarter making the fleet we own actually earn its keep. The downside is bounded, the learning is permanent, and the decision we make in ninety days will be a far better one than the decision we could make today.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Platform Engineering
**From:** Infrastructure Working Group
**Re:** Hardware expansion vs. utilisation improvement for our inference and training workloads

**Summary and recommendation**

We recommend that we spend the next quarter improving utilisation of the hardware we already own, and defer the purchase decision until we have real numbers in hand. This is not a verdict that we have enough hardware — it may well turn out that we don't. It is a judgment that we cannot yet tell the difference between a genuine capacity shortage and a scheduling problem, and the two require very different responses. Buying more machines before we understand our own utilisation pattern risks spending capital to paper over an operational issue that would follow us onto the new hardware anyway.

**Where we stand**

Our current fleet runs at what the dashboards report as roughly 40–45% average utilisation, but that number is doing a lot of work. It averages across the day, across machines, and across job types. Our nightly training runs saturate the cluster; our daytime inference traffic is bursty and mostly idle. The peak-to-trough spread is wide, and peak demand — not average demand — is what actually determines whether people experience queueing. So the honest answer to "are we capacity constrained?" is: sometimes, in ways we haven't carefully characterised.

**Cost**

The purchase option is straightforwardly expensive. New accelerators at current prices would consume most of our remaining annual capital budget, and the depreciation clock starts the moment the boxes arrive. The utilisation option costs mostly engineering time — batching improvements, better queueing, possibly a scheduler upgrade — which is real but smaller, and it's an expense we'd want to make regardless of what we later buy. There's also an asymmetry worth naming: if we improve utilisation and it turns out we still need hardware, we've lost a quarter and gained a better-configured fleet. If we buy hardware and it turns out we didn't need it, we've lost capital we can't easily recover, and we've also inherited the operating burden of machines that sit half-idle.

**Latency**

Latency is where the two options genuinely diverge. Better batching and denser packing raise throughput but tend to add queueing delay at the tail; there is a real tension between squeezing utilisation and keeping p99 response times flat. If our interactive workloads are already latency-sensitive, aggressive consolidation could degrade user experience even as the utilisation graphs look healthier. This is the strongest argument for the buy path, and we should take it seriously. But it's also an argument for measuring first: if we knew how much of our latency budget is actually consumed by scheduling overhead versus raw compute contention, we'd know how much headroom consolidation can safely use.

**Reliability**

Utilisation improvements concentrate load. A fleet running at 85% has less slack to absorb a node failure, a thermal event, or a bad deploy than one loafing along at 45%. Our current spare capacity is, in effect, our redundancy budget, and we should not spend it casually. Any consolidation plan needs an explicit reliability floor — headroom we agree never to consume — rather than treating idle capacity as free money. Conversely, more hardware does improve fault tolerance, and if our single-node failure modes are currently painful, that's a point in favour of expansion that pure utilisation math won't capture.

**Opportunity cost**

The engineering time for utilisation work is time not spent on product work, and that's the real cost of the path I'm recommending. But the purchase path has its own opportunity cost: capital committed to accelerators is capital not available for hiring, tooling, or the next surprise. Hardware also locks us into a generation of technology at what may be a poor point in the price-performance curve. Utilisation work, by contrast, produces knowledge and tooling that remain valuable whatever we later buy.

**Reversibility**

This is the decisive consideration for me. Utilisation improvements are largely reversible — we can relax batching, loosen queueing policy, and return to our current posture if it isn't working. A hardware purchase is not. Once the budget is spent and the machines are racked, our options narrow. When one path is reversible and the other isn't, and when our data is too noisy to be confident, the reversible path is where we should start.

**What we'd do**

Concretely: instrument per-job and per-hour utilisation properly, run a batching and scheduling experiment on one segment of the fleet, and set an explicit reliability floor. Revisit the purchase decision in one quarter with real numbers. If peak demand still exceeds what a well-run fleet can serve, we'll buy — and we'll be able to say exactly why and how much.

I'm aware this recommendation could be wrong in one specific way: if demand is about to step-change (a new product launch, a large customer), the analysis above underweights speed. If we have credible evidence of imminent demand growth, the calculus shifts toward buying now. Absent that, I'd rather earn the purchase than guess at it.
